title: Of custom, and that we should not easily change a law received
paragraphs: Whoever first invented the story of the country woman who, having got used to carrying a young calf in her arms and going on with it every day as it grew, ended up by custom able to carry the full-grown ox, seems to me to have understood the power of custom rightly. For, in truth, custom is a violent and treacherous schoolmistress. Little by little, slyly and unnoticed, she slips in the foot of her authority; but once she has, by this gentle and humble beginning, with the help of time, fixed and established it, she then unmasks a furious and tyrannical face, against which we have no more courage or power even to lift our eyes. We see her, at every turn, forcing and violating the rules of nature:
"Usus efficacissimus rerum omnium magister."
["Custom is the best master of all things." — Pliny, Nat. Hist., xxvi. 2.]

I refer to her on Plato's cave in his Republic, and on the physicians, who so often submit the reasons of their art to her authority — as in the story of the king who, by custom, brought his stomach to such a state as to live on poison, and the girl Albertus reports to have lived on spiders. In that new world of the Indies, great nations were found, and in very different climates, who were of the same diet, kept these creatures and fed them for their tables; as they also did grasshoppers, mice, lizards, and bats; and in a time of scarcity of such delicacies, a toad was sold for six crowns — all which they cooked and dressed with various sauces. Others were found to whom our diet, and the flesh we eat, were poisonous and fatal:
"Consuetudinis magna vis est: pernoctant venatores in nive: in montibus uri se patiuntur: pugiles, caestibus contusi, ne ingemiscunt quidem."

["The power of custom is very great: huntsmen will lie out all night in the snow, or let themselves be burned up by the sun on the mountains; boxers, bruised by the caestus, never utter a groan." — Cicero, Tusc., ii. 17.]

These strange examples will seem less strange if we consider what we have ordinary experience of — how much custom stupefies our senses. We need not go to what is reported of the people about the cataracts of the Nile; nor to what philosophers believe about the music of the spheres — that the bodies of those circles being solid and smooth, and coming to rub against each other, cannot fail to create a marvellous harmony, the changes and cadences of which cause the revolutions and dances of the stars; but that the hearing of all creatures here below, being universally, like that of the Egyptians, deafened and stupefied by the continual noise, cannot, however great, perceive it. Smiths, millers, pewterers, forgemen, and armourers could never live in the perpetual noise of their own trades, did it strike their ears with the same violence it strikes ours.

My perfumed doublet pleases my own scent at first; but after I have worn it three days, it pleases only the bystanders. This is yet stranger: that custom, despite long intermissions and intervals, still has the power to unite and establish the effect of its impressions on our senses, as is plain in those who live near steeples and the frequent ringing of bells. I myself lodge at home in a tower, where every morning and evening a very large bell rings out the Ave Maria; the noise shakes my very tower, and at first seemed insufferable to me; but I am so used to it now that I hear it without any offence, and often without waking at it.

When Plato was reproving a boy for playing at nuts, "You are reproving me," said the boy, "for a very little thing." "Custom," replied Plato, "is no little thing." I find that our greatest vices take their first leaning from our most tender infancy, and that our principal upbringing depends on the nurse. Mothers are mightily pleased to see a child wring the neck of a chicken, or to amuse itself by hurting a dog or a cat. And there are fathers wise enough to take it as a notable mark of a martial spirit when they hear a son insult, or see him domineer over, a poor peasant or a lackey who dares not answer back; and a great sign of wit when they see him cheat and outwit his playfellow by some malicious treachery and deceit. Yet these are the true seeds and roots of cruelty, tyranny, and treason: they bud and put out there, and afterwards shoot up vigorously and grow to a prodigious bulk, cultivated by custom. And it is a very dangerous mistake to excuse these vile inclinations on grounds of the tenderness of their age and the triviality of the subject: first, because it is nature that speaks, whose declaration is then more sincere, and inward thoughts more undisguised, as it is more weak and young; secondly, because the ugliness of cheating does not consist in, or depend on, the difference between crowns and pins. I rather hold it more just to conclude this way: why should he not cheat for crowns since he does it for pins? — than to say, as they do, that they are only playing for pins; they would not do it if it were for money. Children should carefully be taught to abhor vices in their own texture, and the natural ugliness of those vices should be so impressed on them that they may not only avoid them in their actions but, above all, abominate them in their hearts — so that the very thought is hateful to them, with whatever mask they may be disguised.

I know very well, for my own part, that from having been brought up in childhood to a plain and straightforward way of dealing, and from having had an aversion to all manner of trickery and foul play in my childish sports and games (and indeed it should be noted that children's plays are not performed in play, but are to be judged in them as their most serious actions), there is no game so small in which, from my own breast naturally and without study or effort, I have not an extreme aversion to deceit. I shuffle and cut and make as much clatter with the cards, and keep as strict account for farthings, as if it were for double pistoles; when winning or losing against my wife and daughter, it is the same to me as when I play in good earnest with others for large sums. At all times, and in all places, my own eyes are sufficient to watch my fingers; I am not so narrowly watched by anyone else, nor is there anyone I have more respect for.

The other day I saw, at my own house, a little fellow, a native of Nantes, born without arms, who has so well taught his feet to do the services his hands should have done him, that they have half forgotten their natural office; and indeed the fellow calls them his hands. With them he cuts whatever he wants, charges and discharges a pistol, threads a needle, sews, writes, takes off his hat, combs his head, plays cards and dice, and all with as much dexterity as anyone could with proper limbs. The money I gave him — for he gets his living by showing these feats — he took with his foot, as we do with our hand. I have seen another who, while still a boy, flourished a two-handed sword and, if I may say so, handled a halberd with the mere motions of his neck and shoulders for want of hands; tossed them into the air and caught them again, threw a dagger, and cracked a whip as well as any coachman in France.

But the effects of custom are much more manifest in the strange impressions she imprints on our minds, where she meets less resistance. What has she not the power to impose on our judgments and beliefs? Is there any opinion, however fantastical (setting aside the gross impostures of religions, which we see so many great nations and so many understanding men strangely besotted by; for being beyond the reach of human reason, any error is more excusable in those who are not endowed, by divine bounty, with extraordinary illumination from above) — but, of other opinions, are there any so extravagant that she has not planted and established as laws in some part of the world she has chosen to exercise her power upon? Therefore that ancient exclamation was very just:
"Non pudet physicum, id est speculatorem venatoremque naturae, ab animis consuetudine imbutis petere testimonium veritatis?"
["Is it not a shame for a natural philosopher — that is, for an observer and hunter of nature — to seek testimony of the truth from minds prepossessed by custom?" — Cicero, De Natura Deor., i. 30.]

I do believe that no fancy can enter the human imagination, however absurd or ridiculous, that does not meet with some example of public practice, and that our reason does not, accordingly, ground and back up. There are peoples among whom it is the fashion to turn one's back on those you salute, and never look at the man you intend to honour. There is a place where, whenever the king spits, the greatest ladies of his court hold out their hands to receive it; and another nation, where the most eminent men about him stoop to take up his ordure in a linen cloth. Let us squeeze in room for a story here.

A French gentleman was always in the habit of blowing his nose with his fingers (a thing very much against our fashion), and justifying himself for doing so — he was a man famous for witty answers — he asked me what privilege this filthy excrement had, that we should carry about us a fine handkerchief to receive it, and, what is more, afterwards fold it carefully up and carry it all day in our pockets, which, he said, could not but be much more disgusting and offensive than to see it thrown away, as we do with all our other discharges. I found what he said not altogether without reason; and from being frequently in his company, that slovenly action of his at last grew familiar to me — which nevertheless we make faces at when we hear it reported from another country. Miracles appear so according to our ignorance of nature, not according to the essence of nature; continually being accustomed to anything blinds the eye of our judgment. Barbarians are no more a wonder to us than we are to them, and with no more reason, as everyone would admit if, after travelling over those distant examples, men could settle to reflect on and rightly compare them with their own. Human reason is a tincture almost equally infused into all our opinions and manners, of whatever form; infinite in matter, infinite in diversity. But I return to my subject.

There are peoples where, his wife and children excepted, no one speaks to the king except through a tube. In one and the same nation, virgins reveal those parts that modesty should persuade them to hide, while married women carefully cover and conceal them. To which this custom, in another place, has some relation, where chastity, except in marriage, is of no esteem — for unmarried women may prostitute themselves to as many as they please, and being got with child, may lawfully take physic in the sight of everyone, to destroy what they are carrying. And in another place, if a tradesman marries, all of the same trade who are invited to the wedding lie with the bride before him; and the greater the number, the greater is her honour, and the opinion of her stamina and strength. If an officer marries, the same; the same with a labourer, or any man of low rank — but then it belongs to the lord of the place to perform that office; and yet a strict loyalty during marriage is afterwards required. There are places where brothels of young men are kept for the pleasure of women; where wives go to war as well as husbands, and not only share the dangers of battle but also the honours of command. Others where they wear rings not only through their noses, lips, and cheeks, and on their toes, but also heavy gold pieces thrust through their nipples and buttocks; where, while eating, they wipe their fingers on their thighs, their genitals, and the soles of their feet; where children are excluded from inheritance and only brothers and nephews inherit; and elsewhere only nephews, except in the succession of the prince; where, for the regulation of the community of goods and estates observed in the country, certain sovereign magistrates are charged with the universal oversight of agriculture and the distribution of the produce, according to the need of each one; where they mourn the death of children and feast at the death of old men; where they sleep ten or twelve to a bed, men and their wives together; where women whose husbands come to violent ends may marry again, and others not; where the condition of women is held in such contempt that they kill all the native females and buy wives from their neighbours to supply their use; where husbands may repudiate their wives without showing any cause, but wives cannot leave their husbands for any cause whatever; where husbands may sell their wives in case of sterility; where they boil the bodies of their dead and afterwards pound them to a paste, which they mix with their wine and drink; where the most coveted burial is to be eaten by dogs, and elsewhere by birds; where they believe the souls of the blessed live in all manner of liberty, in delightful fields, furnished with every kind of delicacy, and that it is these souls, repeating the words we utter, that we call Echo; where they fight in the water, and shoot their arrows with the most deadly aim while swimming; where, as a sign of submission, they lift up their shoulders and hang down their heads; where they take off their shoes when they enter the king's palace; where the eunuchs who have charge of the sacred women have, moreover, their lips and noses cut off, that they may not be loved; where the priests put out their own eyes, to be better acquainted with their demons and the better to receive their oracles; where everyone makes a deity of what he likes best — the hunter, of a lion or fox; the fisher, of some fish; idols of every human action or passion; where the sun, the moon, and the earth are the principal deities, and the form of taking an oath is to touch the earth while looking up to heaven; where both flesh and fish are eaten raw; where the greatest oath they take is to swear by the name of some dead person of reputation, laying their hand upon his tomb; where the new year's gift the king sends every year to the princes, his vassals, is fire — which being brought, all the old fire is put out, and the neighbouring peoples are obliged to fetch the new, each for themselves, on pain of high treason; where, when the king, to give himself wholly to devotion, retires from his administration (which often happens), his next successor is obliged to do the same, and the right of the kingdom devolves to the third in succession; where they change the form of government as the needs of affairs seem to require, depose the king when they think fit, substituting certain elders to govern in his place, and sometimes transferring power to the hands of the commons; where men and women are both circumcised and also baptised; where the soldier who, in one or several engagements, has been lucky enough to present the king with seven enemy heads is made noble; where they live in the rare and unsociable opinion of the mortality of the soul; where women give birth without pain or fear; where the women wear copper greaves on both legs, and if a louse bites them, are bound in magnanimity to bite it back, and dare not marry until they have first made their king an offering of their virginity, if he is pleased to accept; where the ordinary form of salutation is to put a finger down to the earth and then point it up toward heaven; where men carry burdens upon their heads and women upon their shoulders; where the women make water standing, and the men squatting; where they send their blood as a token of friendship, and offer incense to the men they would honour, as to gods; where, not only to the fourth, but in any other remote degree, kindred are not allowed to marry; where children are four years at nurse, often twelve; in which place, also, it is considered fatal to give a child suck the first day after it is born; where the correction of male children belongs particularly to the fathers, and of girls to the mothers, the punishment being to hang them by the heels in the smoke; where they circumcise the women; where they eat all sorts of herbs without any scruple except for the badness of their smell; where everything is open — the finest houses, furnished in the richest manner, without doors, windows, trunks, or chests to lock, a thief being there punished double what they are in other places; where they crack lice with their teeth like monkeys, and abhor to see them killed with one's nails; where in their whole lives they neither cut their hair nor pare their nails; and, in another place, pare those of the right hand only, letting the left grow for ornament and show; where they let the hair on the right side grow as long as it will, and shave the other; and in neighbouring provinces, some let their hair grow long in front, and some behind, shaving close the rest; where parents let out their children, and husbands their wives, for hire to their guests; where a man may get his own mother with child, and fathers make use of their own daughters or sons without scandal; where, at their solemn feasts, they interchangeably lend their children to one another, without any consideration of blood relation. In one place, men feed on human flesh; in another, it is reputed a pious duty for a man to kill his father at a certain age; elsewhere, fathers dispose of their children while still in the womb, some to be preserved and carefully brought up, others to be abandoned or made away with. Elsewhere old husbands lend their wives to young men; in another place they are held in common without offence; and in one place in particular, the women count it a mark of honour to have as many gay fringed tassels at the hem of their garment as they have lain with men. Moreover, has not custom made a republic of women on their own? Has it not put arms into their hands and made them raise armies and fight battles? And does she not, by her precept alone, teach the most ignorant rabble and make them perfect in things which all the philosophy in the world could never beat into the heads of the wisest men? For we know whole nations where death was not only despised but welcomed with the greatest triumph; where children of seven let themselves be whipped to death without changing countenance; where riches were held in such contempt that the meanest citizen would not have stooped to take up a purse of crowns. And we know regions, very fertile in all manner of provisions, where, nevertheless, the most ordinary diet — and the one they are most pleased with — is only bread, cresses, and water. Did not custom, moreover, work that miracle in Chios that, in seven hundred years, it was never known that any maid or wife committed an act to the prejudice of her honour?

In short, there is nothing, in my opinion, that she does not, or may not, do; and so with very good reason Pindar calls her the ruler of the world. He who was seen beating his father, and was reproved for it, answered that it was the custom of their family: that, in like manner, his father had beaten his grandfather, his grandfather his great-grandfather; "and this," he said, pointing to his son, "when he comes to my age, shall beat me." And the father whom the son dragged and hauled along the streets ordered him to stop at a certain door, for he himself, he said, had dragged his father no farther — that being the utmost limit of the hereditary outrage the sons in their family used to inflict on the fathers. It is as much by custom as by infirmity, says Aristotle, that women tear their hair, bite their nails, and eat coals and earth — and more by custom than nature that men abuse themselves with one another.

The laws of conscience, which we pretend to derive from nature, proceed from custom. Each one, having an inward veneration for the opinions and manners approved and received among his own people, cannot, without very great reluctance, depart from them, nor adopt others without applause. In times past, when the Cretans wished to curse anyone, they prayed the gods to engage him in some bad custom. But the chief effect of custom's power is so to grip and ensnare us that it is hardly in us to disengage ourselves from her clutch, or come back to ourselves enough to consider and weigh the things she commands. To tell the truth, since we suck her in with our milk, and since the face of the world presents itself in this posture to our first sight, it seems as if we were born on condition to follow on this track; and the common fancies we find in repute everywhere around us, infused into our minds with the seed of our fathers, appear to be the most universal and genuine — from which it comes about that whatever is off the hinges of custom is believed to be also off the hinges of reason, how unreasonably for the most part, God knows.

If, as we who study ourselves have learned to do, every man who hears a good saying would immediately consider how it touches his own private case, everyone would find it was not so much a fine saying as a severe lash to the ordinary stupidity of his own judgment. But men receive the precepts and admonitions of truth as directed to the common sort, never to themselves; and instead of applying them to their own habits, they only commit them, very ignorantly and uselessly, to memory. But let us return to the empire of custom.

Such people as have been brought up to liberty, subject to no rule but the authority of their own will, look on every other form of government as monstrous and contrary to nature. Those who are accustomed to monarchy do the same; and whatever opportunity fortune gives them to change, even when they have, with great difficulty, disengaged themselves from one master who was burdensome and grievous to them, they at once run, with the same difficulties, to create another, being unable to take subjection itself into hatred.

It is by the mediation of custom that everyone is content with the place where nature has planted him; and the Highlanders of Scotland no more pine for Touraine than the Scythians for Thessaly. Darius, asking certain Greeks what they would take to adopt the custom of the Indians, of eating the dead bodies of their fathers (for that was their custom, believing they could give them no better, no nobler burial than to bury them in their own bodies), they replied that nothing in the world would induce them to do it. But having also tried to persuade the Indians to leave their custom, and, after the Greek manner, burn the bodies of their fathers, they conceived a still greater horror at the idea. Everyone does the same, for use veils from us the true look of things.
"Nil adeo magnum, nec tam mirabile quidquam Principio, quod non minuant mirarier omnes Paullatim."
["There is nothing at first so grand, so admirable, that by degrees people do not regard with less wonder." — Lucretius, ii. 1027.]

Once, taking it on myself to justify something in use among us, accepted with absolute authority for many leagues round about, and not content, as men commonly do, to establish it merely by force of law and example but inquiring still further into its origin, I found the foundation so weak that I, whose business it was to confirm others, was very near being dissatisfied myself. It is by this same prescription that Plato sets out to cure the unnatural and preposterous loves of his time, treating it as a sovereign remedy — namely, that public opinion condemns them; that poets and all other kinds of writers tell horrible stories about them; a recipe by virtue of which the most beautiful daughters no more allure their fathers' lust, nor brothers of the finest shape and figure their sisters' desire; the very fables of Thyestes, Oedipus, and Macareus, with the harmony of their song, infusing this wholesome opinion and belief into the tender brains of children. Chastity is, in truth, a great and shining virtue, the usefulness of which is sufficiently known; but to treat it, and set it off in its true value, according to nature, is as hard as it is easy to do so according to custom, laws, and precepts. The fundamental and universal reasons are of very obscure and difficult research, and our masters either lightly pass over them, or, not daring even to touch them, throw themselves into the liberty and protection of custom, where they puff themselves up and triumph to their heart's content. Those who refuse to be drawn off from this original source commit a still greater error, and deliver themselves to wild opinions — witness Chrysippus, who, in so many of his writings, scattered the little account he made of incestuous unions, with however near a relation.

Whoever would disengage himself from this violent prejudice of custom would find several things received with absolute and undoubting opinion that have no other support than the grizzled head and wrinkled face of ancient usage. But the mask once off, and things being referred to the decision of truth and reason, he will find his judgment, as it were, altogether overturned, and yet restored to a much surer footing. For example, I shall ask him what can be more strange than to see a people obliged to obey laws they never understood; bound in all their domestic affairs — marriages, gifts, wills, sales, and purchases — to rules they cannot possibly know, being neither written nor published in their own language, and of which they are forced to purchase both the interpretation and the use? Not according to the ingenious opinion of Isocrates, who counselled his king to make the trades and dealings of his subjects free, frank, and profitable to them, and their quarrels and disputes burdensome, weighed down with heavy charges and penalties — but, by a prodigious opinion, to make sale of reason itself, and treat laws as merchandise. I think myself indebted to fortune that, as our historians report, it was a Gascon gentleman, a countryman of mine, who first opposed Charlemagne when he tried to impose on us Latin and imperial laws.

What can be more savage than to see a nation where, by lawful custom, the office of judge is bought and sold, where judgments are paid for in ready money, and where justice may legitimately be denied to him that has not the means to pay — a merchandise in such repute that it creates, in the state, a fourth estate of wrangling lawyers, in addition to the three ancient ones of church, nobility, and people; which fourth estate, having the laws in their own hands and sovereign power over men's lives and fortunes, makes another body separate from the nobility — whence it comes about that there are double laws, those of honour and those of justice, in many things diametrically opposed to one another: the nobles condemning as rigorously the man who pockets an affront as the others do the man who avenges one. By the law of arms, he shall be stripped of all nobility and honour who puts up with an insult; by the civil law, he who avenges his reputation by revenge incurs capital punishment. He who applies to the law for redress of an offence done to his honour, disgraces himself; and he who does not, is censured and punished by the law. Yet of these two so different things, both referring to one head, the one has charge of peace, the other of war; the latter have the profit, the former the honour; the latter the wisdom, the former the virtue; the latter the word, the former the action; the latter justice, the former valour; the latter reason, the former force; the latter the long robe, the former the short — divided between them.

As for indifferent things, like clothes, whoever would try to bring them back to their true use, which is the body's service and convenience, and on which their original grace and fitness depend, will instance — among others — for the most fantastic that can be imagined, our flat caps, the long tail of velvet that hangs down from our women's heads, with its party-coloured trappings; and that vain and futile model of a member we cannot in modesty so much as name, which nevertheless we make a show and parade of in public. These considerations, however, will not persuade any man of understanding to break with the common fashion; on the contrary, it seems to me that all singular and particular fashions are rather marks of folly and vain affectation than of sound reason; and that a wise man, within, should withdraw and retire his soul from the crowd, and there keep it at liberty and in power to judge freely of things, but, as to externals, conform himself absolutely to the fashion of the time. Public society has nothing to do with our thoughts; but the rest — our actions, our labours, our fortunes, and our lives — we are to lend and abandon to its service and to the common opinion, as did that good and great Socrates, who refused to preserve his life by disobedience to the magistrate, though a very wicked and unjust one. For it is the rule of rules, the general law of laws, that everyone observe those of the place in which he lives.
["It is good to obey the laws of one's country." — Excerpta ex Trag. Graecis, Grotio interp., 1626, p. 937.]

Now to another point. It is a very serious question whether any benefit so manifest can come from altering a law that has been received, whatever it be, as to outweigh the danger and inconvenience of altering it — since government is a structure composed of various parts and members so closely joined and united that it is impossible to stir so much as one brick or stone without the whole body feeling it. The legislator of the Thurians ordained that whoever would propose either to abolish an old law or establish a new one should present himself with a halter around his neck to the people, so that, if the innovation he wanted to introduce should not be approved by everyone, he might immediately be hanged; and the Lacedaemonian legislator employed his life in obtaining from his citizens a faithful promise that none of his laws should be violated. The Ephor who so rudely cut the two strings Phrynis had added to music never stopped to examine whether that addition made better harmony, or whether by its means the instrument was fuller and more complete; it was enough for him to condemn the invention because it was a novelty and an alteration of the old fashion. Which is also the meaning of the old rusty sword carried before the magistracy of Marseilles.

For my own part, I have a great aversion to novelty, whatever face or pretence it may bear, and with reason, having been an eyewitness of the great evils it has produced. As for the troubles that for so many years have lain heavily upon us, novelty is not wholly accountable for them; but one can say, with some colour, that it has accidentally produced and brought forth the mischiefs and ruin that have since happened, both without it and against it. It is novelty, principally, that we must blame for these disorders:
"Heu! patior telis vulnera facta meis."
["Alas! The wounds were made by my own weapons." — Ovid, Ep. Phyll. Demophoonti, vers. 48.]

Those who give the first shock to a state are almost naturally the first overwhelmed in its ruin. The fruits of public commotion are seldom enjoyed by the man who first set it going; he beats and disturbs the water for someone else's net. The unity and structure of this monarchy, of this grand edifice, having been ripped and torn in its old age by this thing called innovation, has since shown a rent and given sufficient admittance to such injuries. The royal majesty comes down with greater difficulty from the summit to the middle than it falls and tumbles headlong from the middle to the bottom. But if the inventors do the greater mischief, the imitators are more vicious — to follow examples whose horror and offence they have already felt and punished. And if there can be any honour in ill-doing, these last must yield to the others the glory of contriving and the courage of making the first attempt. All sorts of new disorders easily draw, from this primitive and ever-flowing fountain, examples and precedents to trouble and disrupt our government. We read in our very laws, made as a remedy for this first evil, the beginnings and pretexts of all sorts of wicked enterprises; and what Thucydides said of the civil wars of his time befalls us: that, in favour of public vices, they gave them new and more plausible names for their excuse, sweetening and disguising their true titles — which must be done, forsooth, to reform our conscience and belief:
"Honesta oratio est;"
["Fine words, truly." — Ter. And., i. 1, 114.]
But the best pretext for innovation is of very dangerous consequence:
"Aden nihil motum ex antiquo probabile est."
["We are ever wrong in changing ancient ways." — Livy, xxxiv. 54.]

And, to speak my mind freely, it argues a strange self-love and great presumption to be so fond of one's own opinions that the public peace must be overthrown to establish them, and so many inevitable mischiefs introduced, with so dreadful a corruption of manners as civil war and the changes of state that follow always bring in their train — and to introduce them, in a matter of such high concern, into the bowels of one's own country. Can there be worse husbandry than to set up so many certain and known vices against errors that are only contested and disputable? And are there any worse vices than those committed against a man's own conscience, and the natural light of his own reason? The Senate, in its quarrel with the people over the administration of religion, was bold enough to return this evasion as current coin:
"Ad deos id magis, quam ad se, pertinere: ipsos visuros, ne sacra sua polluantur;"
["Those things belong to the gods to determine rather than to them; let the gods, therefore, take care that their sacred mysteries are not profaned." — Livy, x. 6.]

according to what the oracle answered those of Delphi who, fearing to be invaded by the Persians in the Median war, asked Apollo how they should dispose of the holy treasure of his temple — whether they should hide it, or move it to some other place? He returned them the answer that they should remove nothing from there and only take care of themselves, for he was sufficient to look after what belonged to him.

The Christian religion has all the marks of the utmost utility and justice; but none more manifest than the strict injunction it lays without distinction on everyone to yield absolute obedience to the civil magistrate, and to maintain and defend the laws. Of which what a wonderful example has divine wisdom left us, that to establish the salvation of mankind and to bring about His glorious victory over death and sin, would do so no other way but at the mercy of our ordinary forms of justice — subjecting the progress and outcome of so high and so salutary an effect to the blindness and injustice of our customs and observances; sacrificing the innocent blood of so many of His elect, and so long a loss of so many years, to the maturing of this inestimable fruit? There is a vast difference between the case of one who follows the forms and laws of his country, and one who undertakes to regulate and change them. The first pleads simplicity, obedience, and example for his excuse: whatever he does, it cannot be charged to malice; at the worst it is only misfortune:
"Quis est enim, quem non moveat clarissimis monumentis testata consignataque antiquitas?"
["For who is there whom antiquity, attested and confirmed by the noblest monuments, cannot move?" — Cicero, De Divin., i. 40.]

Besides what Isocrates says — that defect comes nearer to moderation than excess — the other is a much more swaggering gamester; for whoever takes it on himself to choose and alter usurps the authority of judging, and should look well about him, and make it his business to discern clearly the defect of what he would abolish, and the virtue of what he is about to introduce.

This very common consideration is what settled me in my place, and kept even my most extravagant and ungoverned youth under the rein, so as not to burden my shoulders with so great a weight as to make myself responsible for a science of that importance, and to dare in this what, in my better and more mature judgment, I would not have dared in the easiest and most indifferent things I had been instructed in, where the temerity of judging is of no consequence at all. It seemed to me very unjust to subject public and established customs and institutions to the weakness and instability of a private and particular fancy (for private reason has but a private jurisdiction), and to attempt that upon the divine which no government will allow a man to do upon the civil laws; with which, though human reason has much more to do than with the other, yet they are sovereignly judged by their own proper judges, and extreme sufficiency serves only to expound and set forth the law and custom received, not to wrest it, nor to introduce any innovation. If at times divine providence has gone beyond the rules to which it has necessarily bound and obliged us men, it is not to give us any dispensation to do the same. Those are masterstrokes of the divine hand, which we are not to imitate but to admire — extraordinary examples, marks of express and particular purposes, of the order of miracles, presented to us as manifestations of His almightiness, equally above both our rules and our force; which it would be folly and impiety to attempt to represent and imitate, and which we are not to follow but to contemplate with the greatest reverence — acts of His person, and not for us. Cotta very fittingly declares:
"Quum de religione agitur, Ti. Coruncanium, P. Scipionem, P. Scaevolam, pontifices maximos, non Zenonem, aut Cleanthem, aut Chrysippum, sequor."
["When matter of religion is in question, I follow the high priests T. Coruncanius, P. Scipio, P. Scaevola, and not Zeno, Cleanthes, or Chrysippus." — Cicero, De Natura Deor., iii. 2.]

God knows, in the present quarrel of our civil war, where there are a hundred articles to strike out and to put in, great and very considerable, how few there are who can truly boast they have exactly and perfectly weighed and understood the grounds and reasons of either party. It is a number, if it is a number at all, that would be able to give us very little disturbance. But what becomes of all the rest? Under what colours do they march, in what quarter do they lie? Theirs have the same effect as other weak and ill-applied medicines: they have only set the humours they would purge more violently to work, stirred and exasperated by the conflict, and left them still behind. The potion was too weak to purge, but strong enough to weaken us; so that it does not work, but we still keep it inside, and reap nothing from the operation but inward gripes and pains.

So it is, nevertheless, that Fortune, still keeping her authority in defiance of whatever we can do or say, sometimes presents us with a necessity so urgent that the laws must yield and give way a little. And when one opposes the spread of an innovation that thus forces itself in by violence, to keep oneself in every place and in every thing within the bounds and rules against those who have the power, and to whom all things are lawful that may serve to advance their design — who have no other law nor rule but what serves best their own purpose — is a dangerous obligation and an intolerable inequality:
"Aditum nocendi perfido praestat fides,"
["Putting faith in a treacherous person opens the door to harm." — Seneca, Oedip., act iii., verse 686.]

since the ordinary discipline of a healthy state does not provide for these extraordinary accidents: it presupposes a body that holds itself up in its principal members and offices, and a common consent in its obedience and observance. A legitimate procedure is cold, heavy, and constrained, and not fit to make head against a headstrong and unbridled one. It is, to this day, cast in the dish of those two great men, Octavius and Cato, in the two civil wars of Sylla and Caesar, that they would rather suffer their country to undergo the last extremities than relieve their fellow-citizens at the expense of its laws, or be guilty of any innovation. For, in truth, in these last necessities, where there is no other remedy, it would perhaps be more prudent to stoop and yield a little, to receive the blow, than, by opposing without possibility of doing good, to give occasion to violence to trample all under foot; and better to make the laws do what they can, when they cannot do what they would. After this manner did the man who suspended them for twenty-four hours; and he who, for once, shifted a day in the calendar; and the other who, of the month of June, made a second of May. The Lacedaemonians themselves, so religious observers of the laws of their country, being constrained by one of their own edicts which expressly forbade them to choose the same man twice as admiral, and on the other hand, their affairs necessarily requiring that Lysander should again take that command upon him, they made one Aratus admiral — true enough, but with this addition, that Lysander went out as general of the navy. And by the same subtlety, one of their ambassadors being sent to the Athenians to obtain the revocation of some decree, and Pericles pointing out to him that it was forbidden to take down the tablet on which a law had once been engrossed, he advised him only to turn it round, that being not forbidden. And Plutarch praises Philopoemen for this — that, being born to command, he knew how to do it not only according to the laws but also to overrule the laws themselves, when public necessity so required.
